requirement_title: Feature Request: Allow generation of Formatter for a type in a referenced assembly
requirement_text:
# REQ-2129: Feature Request: Allow generation of Formatter for a type in a referenced assembly

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2129
Type: feature

## Requirement

Given Project A (contains `ProjectA.MyType`, has no and cannot have a reference to the MessagePack NuGet package) and Project B (references Project A and MessagePack), the reporter needs a source-generated `IMessagePackFormatter` for `ProjectA.MyType` generated inside Project B.

Proposed solution: add a `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` attribute that works for partial classes implementing `IMessagePackFormatter<T>`:

```csharp
[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]
partial class MyObjectFormatter: IMessagePackFormatter<MyObject>;
```

The class does not need a body; the implementation is source-generated by `MessagePack.SourceGenerator.MessagePackGenerator` as usual.

For attribute-based property keys and other settings (such as Union), the issue lists three alternatives: (1) use `System.Runtime.Serialization.DataMember` and related attributes; (2) let the generator and analyzers work with user-defined copies of the MessagePack attributes; (3) source-generate the attributes themselves via `RegisterPostInitializationOutput`.

Motivation: Project A is a NuGet library that should stay minimal with zero dependencies.

## Acceptance criteria

- A `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` attribute exists and can be applied to a partial class implementing `IMessagePackFormatter<T>`.
- The source generator emits the formatter implementation for `T` inside the annotated class, in the assembly that declares the class (Project B), even when `T` is declared in a referenced assembly.
- The annotated class may be declared without a body (`partial class X : IMessagePackFormatter<T>;`).
- `T` needs no MessagePack attributes: without `[DataContract]` or `[MessagePackObject]` on `T` the generated formatter uses contractless behaviour over public members. (derived from maintainer comment)
- If `T` does carry MessagePack attributes, they are honoured. (derived from maintainer comment)
- Private members are not required to be serialized; only public members are in scope. (derived from maintainer comment)
- Project A needs no reference to the MessagePack package. (derived)

## Notes from discussion

- AArnott: "We might simplistically say this only works in 'contractless' mode, such that you need no attributes on it at all. If there are attributes on it, fine, we'll use them. But if there is no `[DataContract]` or `[MessagePackObject]` attribute on the type, go contractless by default."
- AArnott on prerequisite: "Does ProjectA.MyType requires only `public` members to be serialized? That seems a prerequisite for anything here." Reporter: yes.
- AArnott is not a fan of a `PropertyKeys` dictionary on the formatter, and warns that copying attributes into Project A breaks reflection-based (dynamic resolver) mode.
- AArnott suggested a surrogate-type design: `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter(SurrogateType = typeof(ProjectASurrogate))]`, keys mapped by property name; reporter: "Looks good." No design was settled in the thread.

findings.claim: The acceptance criteria say that if `T` carries MessagePack attributes, they are honoured. They also say contractless mode applies only when `T` has no `[DataContract]` and no `[MessagePackObject]`. Without a surrogate, `Collect` always calls `CreateContractlessMembers`, which never reads `T`'s attributes. As a result, `[MessagePackObject]` with `[Key(n)]`, `[IgnoreMember]`, `[DataContract]`, `[DataMember]` and `[IgnoreDataMember]` on `T` are all ignored. An `[IgnoreMember]` property is still serialized, and integer keys become string-keyed map entries.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.GeneratedFormatterHonoursTypeAttributesTests. HonoursIgnoreMemberOnMessagePackObjectType expects the `[IgnoreMember]` member `Secret` to be absent from the generated formatter. HonoursDataContractMembership expects the non-`[DataMember]` property `Extra` to be absent. On head both appear because contractless mode picks them up, so both tests fail.

findings.claim: The timestamp32 guard now tests the low 32 bits instead of the high 32 bits. A DateTime whose seconds value is a multiple of 2^32 (for example 0, the Unix epoch) but carries nanoseconds takes the 6-byte timestamp32 path. It is written as (uint)data64 = 0, so the sub-second part is lost: 1970-01-01T00:00:00.5Z round-trips as 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. Conversely, every whole-second DateTime that used to be timestamp32 (1970..2106 with ns == 0) is now written as timestamp64, which changes the wire bytes. This edit is unrelated to REQ-2129.

receipt_plan.detail: Run GeneratedFormatterLogicReceipts.DateTimeWithSubSecondAtEpochRoundTrips (round-trip loses 500 ms on head) and GeneratedFormatterLogicReceipts.WholeSecondDateTimeUsesTimestamp32 (expects d6 ff 00 00 00 01; head emits a 10-byte timestamp64).

findings.claim: When SurrogateType is null, the collector always uses CreateContractlessMembers, which reads every public read-write member. Any [MessagePackObject]/[Key]/[IgnoreMember] (or DataContract/DataMember/IgnoreDataMember) annotations on T are never consulted. A referenced type with [MessagePackObject] { [Key(0)] Value; [IgnoreMember] Secret } therefore gets a string-keyed map formatter that also serializes Secret. This violates the acceptance criterion 'If T does carry MessagePack attributes, they are honoured', and the output is wire-incompatible with T's own contract.

receipt_plan.detail: Run GeneratedFormatterLogicReceipts.MessagePackAttributesOnReferencedTypeAreHonoured: Project A declares [MessagePackObject] MyType with [IgnoreMember] Secret, and Project B declares [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] partial MyTypeFormatter. On head the generated source references Secret.

findings.claim: needsCast compares m.Name against "OnBeforeSerialize"/"OnAfterDeserialize" for methods with ExplicitInterfaceImplementations. Roslyn names explicit implementations with the interface prefix ('MessagePack.IMessagePackSerializationCallbackReceiver.OnBeforeSerialize'), so the check is never true. It also only inspects type.GetMembers(), not base types. A data type that implements the callback receiver explicitly gets generated code calling value.OnBeforeSerialize() directly, which fails with CS1061.

hunches.claim: This change inverts the timestamp64 range check. The requirement asks for nothing in the runtime serializer. The original check `(data64 & 0xffffffff00000000) == 0` selected the 6-byte timestamp32 form only when the upper 32 bits (nanoseconds and the high seconds bits) were zero. The new check `(data64 & 0x00000000ffffffff) == 0` selects it whenever the low 32 bits of seconds are zero, then writes only those low 32 bits. Example: `DateTime.UnixEpoch.AddTicks(1)` has seconds = 0 and nanoseconds = 100, and is written as timestamp32 value 0, so the nanoseconds are silently lost. Ordinary DateTimes now take the 10-byte timestamp64 form instead of 6 bytes, which changes the wire format.

receipt_plan.detail: Serialize `new DateTime(2020,1,1,0,0,0,DateTimeKind.Utc)` and `DateTime.UnixEpoch.AddTicks(1)` with `MessagePackSerializer.Serialize` using base-built and head-built MessagePack.dll, then compare the bytes. Base gives `d6 ff ...` (6 bytes) for the first and `d7 ff ...` for the second. Head gives 10 bytes for the first and `d6 ff 00 00 00 00` for the second. Round-trip `DateTime.UnixEpoch.AddTicks(1)` on head; it deserializes as `UnixEpoch`.

hunches.claim: The requirement says 'contractless behaviour over public members', and the ledger (L3) ties contractless to `ContractlessStandardResolver`. That resolver serializes public get-only members and can deserialize through a parameterized constructor. The new collector instead keeps only public read-write members. It also rejects any class without an accessible parameterless constructor by reporting MsgPack007 (lines 77-81). Immutable or record-like types from Project A therefore lose members or cannot get a formatter at all.

receipt_plan.detail: Generator test: Project A declares `public class P { public P(int id) { Id = id; } public int Id { get; } }`, and Project B declares `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] partial class PFormatter : IMessagePackFormatter<ProjectA.P>;`. On head the generator emits no formatter and reports MsgPack007, whereas `ContractlessStandardResolver` round-trips `P`.

hunches.claim: The timestamp writer mask was changed from 0xffffffff00000000 to 0x00000000ffffffff. This is unrelated to the requirement and breaks the wire format. Timestamps with nanoseconds==0 and seconds<2^32 should use the 4-byte timestamp32 form, but now take the 8-byte path or are mis-encoded. Timestamps with nonzero nanoseconds can hit the 6-byte branch and lose data. This changes serialized bytes for every DateTime and DateTimeOffset user.

receipt_plan.detail: Serialize DateTime(2020,1,1,0,0,0,Utc) and DateTime(2020,1,1,0,0,0,Utc).AddTicks(1230) with base-built and head-built MessagePack, then compare bytes. Base gives d6 ff + 4 bytes; head gives a different encoding. Also run the existing Timestamp round-trip tests.

hunches.claim: New analyzer errors MsgPack019-022 are added to SupportedDiagnostics, but the AnalyzerReleases.Unshipped.md hunk is missing. The RS2000 release-tracking analyzer will flag the unlisted IDs, which breaks builds that treat warnings as errors. The new diagnostics are reported only by the generator and are never wired into the analyzer.

receipt_plan.detail: Build MessagePack.SourceGenerator and check for RS2000 errors for MsgPack019-022. Also run the analyzer tests that enumerate SupportedDiagnostics against the release-tracking file.

hunches.claim: The generator passes IsUserDeclaredFormatter output through the shared templates, which emit 'partial class Name' with no accessibility modifier. They also emit the type's nesting and namespace wrappers. If the user's class is declared 'public partial class' or 'sealed', the generated half does not conflict, but the resolver registration and the generated resolver still reference the formatter. A user-declared formatter with its own members, such as a Serialize method, will collide. Existing source-generated formatters are unchanged, but the shared templates were modified. Snapshot output for existing types must be verified byte-identical.

receipt_plan.detail: Rerun the generator snapshot tests for existing [MessagePackObject] types and confirm that the output is identical, including the whitespace produced by the changed template line.

hunches.claim: The contractless mode emits string keys but sorts members alphabetically and ignores read-only members, so wire order differs from ContractlessStandardResolver (declaration order, including getter-only members with constructors). Users who switch from the dynamic contractless resolver to this formatter get different map key order and a different member set.

receipt_plan.detail: Serialize a type with public properties Zeta and Alpha, plus a get-only property, using ContractlessStandardResolver and the generated formatter. Compare the bytes.

hunches.claim: The timestamp writer mask in WriteTimestamp was changed from 0xffffffff00000000L to 0x00000000ffffffffL. The timestamp32 branch (6 bytes) is now chosen when the low 32 bits are zero rather than when the high 32 bits are zero. Seconds-only values (nanoseconds == 0) get routed to the 8-byte timestamp64 format, and values whose low 32 bits are zero are written as timestamp32 with the seconds truncated. This is an unrelated change to the serializer runtime that silently corrupts DateTime/timestamp data. It can also cause wrong data to be accepted or emitted across trust boundaries. The change has nothing to do with REQ-2129.

receipt_plan.detail: Serialize DateTime values such as 1970-01-01T00:00:01Z (seconds=1, ns=0) and a value with seconds=0x100000000-ish (low 32 bits zero) with the base-built and head-built code. Compare the bytes. A round-trip test of the timestamp32 and timestamp64 boundaries fails on head. Also assert that the first value is still encoded as timestamp32 (0xd6).

hunches.claim: The change edits the runtime Timestamp writer in MessagePackPrimitives.Writers.cs, which is unrelated to REQ-2129. It flips the mask from 0xffffffff00000000 to 0x00000000ffffffff. The timestamp32 fast path is used only when the upper 32 bits are zero, so the new mask selects the wrong encoding and corrupts DateTime serialization. Numeric serialization is recorded as bug-prone in L16.

receipt_plan.detail: Serialize a DateTime with nonzero nanoseconds, such as 2020-01-01T00:00:00.5Z, and one with zero nanoseconds. Round-trip both, and byte-diff against the base build. The existing timestamp tests should fail.

hunches.claim: The README and the attribute doc describe the contractless and surrogate-less formatter as serializing members under their names as string keys. Members are sorted by name and given int keys, but those are ignored for string-key maps. Contractless mode in this product also honours attributes on T, per the requirement: 'If T does carry MessagePack attributes, they are honoured'. The collector ignores [DataContract], [MessagePackObject], [Key] and [IgnoreMember] on T entirely. This is a requirement gap.

receipt_plan.detail: Add an external type with [IgnoreMember] or [Key(0)] members in a MessagePack-referencing library. Declare a generated formatter with no surrogate and assert that the attributes are honoured. It currently serializes all public members as string keys.

hunches.claim: The change flips the mask in the timestamp-encoding branch (0xffffffff00000000L -> 0x00000000ffffffffL), an unrelated serializer-runtime edit. It has no test, and the generated-formatter tests do not touch Timestamp encoding. Any mutation or revert of this line survives the change's tests, and the new behavior would write timestamp32 for the wrong inputs.

ExternalPerson covers the read-only property skip, but no test covers public fields, non-public setters, static members, indexers, or base-class members. Mutating IsPublicReadWrite (for example dropping the SetMethod check or the field IsReadOnly check) or GetInstanceMembers would survive.

hunches.claim: The generated formatter's observable behavior is not covered for requirement cases that are tested by neither the diagnostic tests nor the execution tests. The diagnostic tests never include a passing case where the generator emits a formatter, so there is no snapshot of generated text. There is also no test that T's own [MessagePackObject]/[DataContract] attributes are honoured. The requirement says these must be honoured, but the collector ignores them completely.

receipt_plan.detail: Add a type with [MessagePackObject] and [Key(n)] attributes plus a [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] over it, then assert that the keys are honoured. The test would fail because CreateContractlessMembers ignores attributes.

hunches.claim: The diagnostics are tested only for MsgPack019, 020, 021, 022 and the mixed-keys case. There are no tests for the missing parameterless constructor case (NoDeserializingConstructor), the inaccessible type case, the generic type case, the struct case in MsgPack021, the MemberNeedsKey case, or duplicate keys (KeysMustBeUnique). The guards that produce these diagnostics can be removed without any test failing. The mixed-keys test expects MsgPack005 only at one location, and it gets passed through an analyzer reporting path, not necessarily the generator's.

hunches.claim: The tests may not distinguish the string-key surrogate path from the contractless path. SurrogateControlsKeysAndMembership uses int keys only. The branch that creates string-keyed surrogate members, `intKey: members.Count, stringKey: (string)key`, is never executed at runtime, so mutating it to use target.Name would survive.

receipt_plan.detail: GeneratedFormatterCollector.cs:170 delete-statement: replace stringKey: (string)key with stringKey: target.Name; expected to survive because the only runtime surrogate (ExternalWidgetSurrogate) uses integer keys.

hunches.claim: The GeneratorUtilities.cs filter excluding [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] classes from hand-written-formatter registration has no direct assertion. GeneratedFormattersAreRegisteredInGeneratedResolver would still pass if the exclusion were removed, because GetFormatter would return the same instance type. Removing the filter could cause a duplicate registration, but nothing tests for it.

receipt_plan.detail: GeneratorUtilities.cs:38 remove-guard: delete the `!symbol.GetAttributes().Any(...)` condition; expected to survive because the tests only check the resolver returns the formatter type, not that registration is unique or free of duplicates.

hunches.claim: The new template branch `Info.IsUserDeclaredFormatter ? "partial class" : "internal sealed class"` is covered only by an execution test on the string-key path. The int-key path, which is used by the surrogate, is separately covered. No snapshot test verifies the generated declaration, such as accessibility matching the user's declaration. The user's partial class can be public while the emitted part declares no modifier.

receipt_plan.detail: Run the generator snapshot tests for a [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] class and confirm the emitted `partial class` declaration; there is currently no verifying snapshot.

hunches.claim: IsPartial checks only the formatter's own declaration. A [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] class nested inside a non-partial outer class (or inside a struct) passes validation with no MsgPack019. If the template's nesting emission re-opens the containing type as 'partial class Outer', the generated code fails with CS0260 or a kind mismatch instead of a diagnostic.

receipt_plan.detail: GeneratedFormatterCollector.IsPartial inspects only formatter.DeclaringSyntaxReferences, never formatter.ContainingType chain; template uses EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces for Info.Formatter = QualifiedNamedTypeName(user formatter).

hunches.claim: If T is declared in the same compilation with [MessagePackObject], the regular TypeCollector already produces an ObjectSerializationInfo for T. The generated-formatter path adds a second ObjectInfo for the same data type. Nothing dedupes them, so the resolver can register two formatters for T (a duplicate switch case or ambiguous registration), and the two use different contracts.

receipt_plan.detail: MessagePackGenerator adds generatedModel to modelPerType unconditionally after Collect(typeSymbol) for messagePackObjectTypes; there is no check that the data type was already collected.

hunches.claim: The generated-formatter collector builds ObjectSerializationInfo without applying the MessagePackSecurity-related collision protections or the existing analyzer checks for members. Contractless mode serializes every public read-write member, including members of the third-party type that are not intended for serialization. Deserialization into types with callbacks or setters is reachable from untrusted data. This is the same exposure as ContractlessStandardResolver, but it is opt-in and documented, so it is only a low concern.

receipt_plan.detail: Read CreateContractlessMembers and Collect. Members are emitted without any depth or untrusted-data hooks, relying on the generated template to call options.Security.DepthStep. Confirm this by regenerating a snapshot for a [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] class and checking for DepthStep and Deserialize.

However, the diagnostics are raised only from the generator, not from MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer's analysis. The analyzer's Initialize registers no action for them, so the analyzer never reports the diagnostics it declares. This is a convention mismatch.

In `TypeCollector.CollectCore`, after the custom-formatter, enum and generic checks, a non-generic type whose symbol is metadata-only exits with a bare `if (type.Locations[0].IsInMetadata) { return; }` (TypeCollector.cs:367-370), so no MsgPack003/004/005 diagnostic and no generated formatter appear for it. The defining assembly owns validating and formatting its own types (rationale inferred: the code has no comment). A missing diagnostic or formatter for such a type is not a defect. (source: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs:367) (would-be finding: The change deliberately generates formatters for types from referenced assemblies via a separate GeneratedFormatterCollector, while TypeCollector.CollectCore still skips metadata-only types. This is consistent with L15, which says the TypeCollector skip is deliberate. The new path is opt-in and bypasses that skip.)

interpretations.label: A
interpretations.summary: Add [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] with an optional SurrogateType property, where a user-defined surrogate type in Project B mirrors T's shape and keys are mapped by property name, so attribute-based keys and Union settings can be supplied without touching Project A. Code: Attribute has a SurrogateType property; generator reads keys/union attributes from the surrogate and emits conversion code between T and the surrogate, which the contractless-only reading would not do.

interpretations.label: B
interpretations.summary: Add [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] for a partial class implementing IMessagePackFormatter<T>, generating a contractless formatter over T's public members (honouring any MessagePack attributes present) in the declaring assembly, with no surrogate type. Code: Generator discovers classes with the attribute, reads T from the IMessagePackFormatter<T> interface, and emits Serialize/Deserialize directly for T's public members, defaulting to contractless when T has no [MessagePackObject]/[DataContract]; no SurrogateType property.
